🚨 Ready to see patients, but not getting paid? That's the reality many providers face due to credentialing delays.

Credentialing delays are becoming a bigger challenge than ever.

Many insurance carriers are taking months to complete credentialing applications, leaving providers unable to bill for services despite being fully licensed and ready to practice.

A few ways to help prevent delays:
✔️ Keep your CAQH profile updated
 ✔️ Ensure provider information is consistent across all applications
 ✔️ Start the credentialing process well before a provider's start date
 ✔️ Follow up regularly with insurance carriers

At NIHC Group, we help healthcare providers navigate the credentialing process so they can focus on patient care while we handle the details.

💬 Have you experienced credentialing delays? What has been your biggest challenge?

We got credentialed two years ago. Why is a claim suddenly denying?

Because credentialing expires. Most payers require recredentialing every 2–3 years, and the industry recently shortened that verification window further. If nobody owns that calendar, it lapses quietly — and claims start denying with zero warning.

Credzonic — www.credzonic.com

items.postText:
Postpartum psychosis (PPP) is real. And it very well could be the reason three beautiful children are dead. It's also the reason I started speaking at all.

Lindsay Clancy's trial ended in a mistrial, and at the end of this month the Commonwealth and courts decides what comes next… maybe a second trial. I've watched the whole conversation shift. We went from "she did it," to the internet being absolutely convinced Patrick did it, to her denying he had anything to do with it, to Reddington asking for an acquittal. And somehow we're right back at square one.

We still don't know the full truth. But I do know psychosis is real. I've lived it more than once. Postpartum, and later medication-induced, which honestly felt different. Both were terrifying.

So before anything else, I want to be really clear. This is not an excuse. Psychosis doesn't give anyone a pass to kill their kids. Not Lindsay, not me, not anyone. But we can't treat what we don't understand, and we won't understand it until we actually listen to the people who've lived it. Somebody needs to say out loud what postpartum psychosis is like from the inside. I'm hoping my share can help prevent this from ever happening to another family.

I'll be honest… this is almost unbearable to post. I've written and rewritten it. I've thought about how it might change the way people see me. But I keep coming back to the same thing: if it helps even one woman, it's worth whatever it costs me. So here it is.

I had it. Never diagnosed. Nobody would listen.

I heard voices. I saw shadows in my house. They told me my husband was going to kill my daughter. That he was going to kill me. That he was waiting for his chance to hurt me, that I was nothing but a surrogate to him, that I was worthless, that I should be dead. And I believed every word. I was "with it" enough to know it wasn't real… and it was still one of the scariest, most helpless, disempowering experiences of my life. I knew and I didn't know, at the same time. I still can't make that make sense, even now.

That's what people don't understand. It doesn't feel like symptoms. It feels like you're the only person in the house who can see what's really happening. It feels like you're being gaslit by yourself, like you're going crazy, and like no one will ever believe you.

It's so real and so delusional at once that you start doubting everything you've ever known. I lost friends. Close friends, ones who were passionate about mental health. I lost babysitters. And very obviously, I lost my mind. You can see it in photos from back then, which is even harder to bear.

There were nights I locked myself in the bathroom with my baby and screamed. Screamed. Covering her ears while my husband knocked gently on the other side of the door, because I was certain he was breaking it down to get to us.

He was just knocking. Frustrated, scared, confused. But just knocking.

I ripped one of my favorite children's books to shreds with my bare hands and threw things around the house, because the voices had convinced me he'd only made a baby with me so he could take her away. I hurt myself. I cried uncontrollably, and I never got a break because he had to work. I had no real help. I drove him off with the cruelest things I could find… and then screamed like I was dying because he was leaving me. I thought I was protecting myself. Protecting our family.

And once (I've said this one publicly before, but never with the why) I told my husband to kill himself. He'd just told me he wanted to leave because he couldn't handle the crazy behavior anymore.

He tried. I chased him down while on the phone with 911, and he stopped. He was admitted for three days, and he came back. I knew something had to change. I tried anxiety meds, more therapy, and nothing really helped. The voices kept coming back… less and less with time. Honestly, stopping breastfeeding was the biggest help. Years later I was diagnosed with MCAS, and I learned we'd had toxic black mold in our home. I believe that played a role too, alongside the pregnancy and postpartum hormones.

I carried this pain for years without ever publicly explaining it. I let people think whatever they thought about my time as a new mom. I did "the work," and slowly built the tribe I have now. In my opinion, my COVID birth was the trigger. But looking back, it wasn't just one thing. Sometimes things happen and we never find real answers. I wasn't a woman with a cruel streak. I was a woman who had lost hold of reality, whose mind had spent months telling her this man was a threat to her child, and I acted out in the only ways I knew how, no matter how toxic or shameful they were. That doesn't make it okay. Nothing makes it okay.

He carries what happened that night, and so do I. But it wasn't malice, love. It was madness. And there's a difference, even when the damage is the same. We gave all of it to Jesus… those nights, those years, every piece we couldn't carry ourselves. He helped me forgive myself. Therapy and a lot of repair helped us rebuild our life.

But here's what should scare people. I was practicing as a licensed psychotherapist through some of it. Not at its height, because I was on maternity leave then. But while it was still hard, I was sitting with clients, giving good, sound care and solid advice to help them through their problems.

After work, a switch would flip and I'd be someone else for a while… and then it would flip back and I'd be fine. Mornings and evenings were the hardest… the transition times. I checked the baby monitor two hundred times a day and didn't even know that was strange.

I was in EMDR. In talk therapy. Seeing an LMFT. Three skilled providers, all experienced with postpartum and trauma, and every single one called it anxiety. A trauma response to a traumatic birth. No concerns for anyone's safety, because I could intellectualize everything so succinctly, and because I showed remorse (I was remorseful). That's what came out of my mouth by the time I got to the chair. The thoughts and feelings had already passed. If there'd been cameras in my house, maybe someone would have intervened.

That's a big part of why I don't hold licensure in the reverence I once did. All of it was missed, and I lost respect for the system. I also knew 30 clients a week was too much for me, so I moved into part-time coaching. I learned my boundaries and my limits, and I stopped pushing past them just to survive. I burned out three times in that process. The hardest pill to swallow was this: I was credentialed, supervised, and ethically bound to do no harm, which I didn't, not to my clients. And I was completely psychotic in my home life, and not one piece of that framework caught it. The letters after your name don't make you safe, and they don't make you seen. There's a whole industry built on the idea that they do, but that's a different post. This is just my story.

I never told anyone about the voices. Not once. Because I knew they weren't real… and "people who hear voices think they're real, right?" I was completely certain that the second I said it out loud, they'd take my daughter from me. Looking back, I lied by omission. I was in such deep denial of my own experience, and I went home every day to a world none of them knew existed. A year and a half of that before I finally found peace, and light in the darkness.

I don't know exactly when it lifted. I noticed it arriving, and I noticed it leaving, but it was like an insidious being that never announced itself through anything but my own thoughts and behavior. I call them demons, and thank God they're gone. Somewhere in the prayer, the somatic work, the NLP, some private psychedelic healing, and five days alone at a women's retreat when my girl was a year and a half old, I came back different. That was years ago now. So much has changed. That woman isn't who I am anymore, but I know I hurt people, including myself.

My belief saved me. Saved us. That's the rock I speak from now. And so much of what brought me back, I use with my own clients in mentorship and coaching, alongside everything I learned as a formerly licensed, thoroughly trained psychotherapist. That's why I've dedicated my life to teaching people how to come back from this kind of intense dysregulation. I teach the tools so you can find your own salvation, whatever that looks like for you… and learn to help yourself in the process. I had to find my own way back, and I don't want anyone else finding it alone.

My story is brighter than Lindsay's. My daughter is thriving, and she has a mother who is fully here. I didn't do the unspeakable, and I thank God every day for that.

So when I look at a mother in a case like this, I don't feel the urge to call her a monster. She had a monster guiding her, and she's a victim of it too. And honestly? I feel sick. I feel compassion, and sadness. Because I know how narrow that ledge is. And I know how many people walk right past a woman standing on it… turning a blind eye, or talking about how she doesn't deserve to be a mom.

I'm not excusing anything. Not a single thing, not in my story and not in hers. Children died. That stays unbearable, and it should. I don't support it, condone it, or speak of it lightly. It's heartbreaking. But if the firsthand story of someone who lived through psychosis and found her way out can help others in the same trenches, then I've done my work.

So if a woman tells you something is wrong in her mind after a baby, believe her the first time. I kept telling my husband "something is wrong," and he just didn't know what to do. I said it to providers, to doctors, and no one seemed to care, or have the tools to really help. That's life with serious mental illness for so many. Maybe that's what happened with Lindsay. Who knows.

And if she comes to you for help, ask the harder question. Ask if she's seeing things. Hearing things. Because she will not offer it up, love. She's too afraid of what happens when she does. Reassure her that she won't lose her child, that she'll finally get the support she needs. Because it's not worth losing a child permanently. I'm grateful I never had to "go there," and can speak from what I learned instead.

I know there's so much fear around getting help. So please look at my pinned post. I've gathered options to help bring you or your loved one back when someone isn't in an active psychotic episode but is still showing symptoms, because hospitals aren't equipped to hold anyone forever. These are real tools you can use alongside medical care. It's a full list, and it's always growing.

And if this is you, reading this right now… please hear me.

Reach out. Tell someone. Today, if you can.

This is not normal, and you are not meant to white-knuckle your way through it alone. What's happening to you is a medical emergency that deserves real care. Not silence. Not shame.

You are not alone in this. There are so many more of us than anyone talks about. We just don't say it out loud, for every single reason I've spent this whole post explaining.

And you are not a monster, love. You are a woman whose brain is doing something to her that she did not choose and cannot fix by trying harder. Those are not the same thing. They have never been the same thing.

Please tell someone. Please let yourself be helped.

I got lucky. That's the whole truth of it. Not stronger. Not better. Lucky.

Whatever you believe about the Clancy case, please share awareness of this debilitating illness. Prevention and intervention save lives.

You never know who's quietly drowning in it. Your one share could be the thing that reaches her. It can genuinely save lives… maybe more than one.

💛 National Maternal Mental Health Hotline: call or text 1-833-TLC-MAMA (1-833-852-6262), 24/7
💛 Postpartum Support International HelpLine: 1-800-944-4773, staffed by people who understand this specifically (support and resources, not a crisis line)
💛 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: call or text anytime, 24/7
💛 If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911

In reverence. In love. In peace. 🧡

The overwhelm you’re carrying.
The feeling-like-crap that won’t seem to leave.
The answer that you’re not exactly sure whether or not you want to receive.
Beloved,
Today I pray you give yourself grace in the hard.
The reality that is now yours to live.
The decision that you must make.
The wait that seems like it’s taking forever, or the fact that the time has come, and so now you kinda wish you could wait a bit longer.
Beloved,
Today I pray you give yourself grace in the hard.
The news that you’re still processing.
The tears that you’re desperately trying to find a place for inside instead of letting them fall, because you feel so dumb/silly/ridiculous for crying about what you’re certain most people would call a small thing, but of course to you it feels huge.
The hard.
The break-up, the parting of ways, the letting go of what was and being okay with it, trying your best to simply move on while still holding gratitude for what was in that season.
The path before you that you never expected at this stage in your life and so you’ve decided that walking it by faith is the best course of action.
The nights that seem endless.
The days that are long.
The moments you wish never would’ve been and the fear of those still up ahead.
The hard.
Beloved,
Today I pray you give yourself grace in the hard.
Not denying it, I know it is real.
Instead, giving yourself what it is that you need in the midst of it.
Yes.
Give yourself grace in the form of patience.
Give yourself grace in the form of rest, or play.
Give yourself grace in the form of writing it out, or talking it out with a good trusted friend.
Give yourself grace in the form of a great cup of coffee and savor each and every dark sip.
Give yourself grace in the form of prayer, and be real, ok? After all, God already knows.
Beloved,
Today I pray you give yourself grace in the hard.
And remind yourself that things will not always be hard…and you will get through it…and you are seen, heard, known, and loved…through each and every ounce of it.
You sure are.
XO.

7:14 Prayer

Good morning Jesus.  To call out Your Name, my heart leaps for joy knowing You are ready to continue our journey together.  We are forever making daily decisions and setting priorities for our life.  We pretty much do what we want to do with our lives.  Time is always short, therefore, we do what we have set the highest priorities. Most days my chronological triage could be better by putting the most life-giving pursuits first place.  The Apostle Paul struggled with the same notion .  The Message version of Philippians 3: 7 is life-giving:  “The very credentials these people are waving around as something special, I’m tearing up and throwing out with the trash—along with everything else I used to take credit for. And why? Because of Christ. Yes, all the things I once thought were so important are gone from my life. Compared to the high privilege of knowing Christ Jesus as my Master, firsthand, everything I once thought I had going for me is insignificant—dog dung. I’ve dumped it all in the trash so that I could embrace Christ and be embraced by him. I didn’t want some petty, inferior brand of righteousness that comes from keeping a list of rules when I could get the robust kind that comes from trusting Christ—God’s righteousness.” (MSG).  One of God’s greatest promises is found in Matthew 6:33: “But seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.” (NIV).  My experience many times over has proven God meets our needs abundantly by putting God as our highest pursuit.  To know Jesus is the surpassing value of my life.  All other things are worthless compared to the single value of knowing Jesus as Lord.   When important things like marriage, children, ministry, and security slip into first place prepare for pain.  God deserves first place above all other endeavors.  An amazing thing happens, or as Gomer Pyle use to say: “surprise, surprise,” one becomes the best spouse, parent, minister living in the confidence, security and power of God.  Saint of God, may knowing Jesus be the passion of your life! By the power of God’s grace at work in you,  we press on toward the goal of knowing, loving, and serving Jesus our Lord, in whose Name I pray.  Amen!

GRACE IS THE BEGINNING, THE CONSUMMATION, AND THE CROWN.
Main Text: Ephesians 2:8–9; 1 Corinthians 15:10; 2 Corinthians 12:9
Theme: 
Grace is not merely what starts us—it is what sustains us, completes us, and ultimately crowns what God has done in us.

There are some things in God that we begin by faith, continue by grace, and finish by His power.
Grace is the beginning. Grace is the journey. Grace is the consummation. And grace is the crown.
Ephesians 2:8 says, “For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith—and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God.”
Before you had a testimony, there was grace.
Before you had a ministry, there was grace.
Before anyone recognized you, God had already touched your life with grace.
You did not begin because you were perfect. You began because God was gracious.
You did not survive because you were strong enough. You survived because grace carried you.
And when your journey is finally complete, you will not stand before God saying, “Look at what I accomplished.” You will bow and say, “Look what the grace of God has done!”

1. GRACE IS THE BEGINNING.
Grace introduces us to God.
Paul reminds us in 1 Corinthians 15:10:
“But by the grace of God I am what I am.”
Paul understood something powerful: his identity was not merely the product of his effort; it was the evidence of God's grace.
Think about Peter.
Peter denied Jesus three times. Yet Jesus did not cancel his destiny.
In John 21, Jesus restored Peter and entrusted him with responsibility: “Feed my sheep.”
Peter's failure was real, but grace was greater.
That means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Grace can meet you at your lowest point and begin something new in you.
The prodigal son began his journey home when he was still broken.
The thief on the cross encountered grace when he had nothing left to offer.
Saul encountered Jesus while travelling in the wrong direction.
Grace does not wait until you become worthy.
Grace finds you, changes you, and begins God's work in you.
ILLUSTRATION: THE EMPTY HANDS
Imagine a person standing before a king with empty hands.
He has no achievement to present. No credentials. No payment.
Yet the king says, “I choose to give you this.”
That is grace.
Grace is receiving what you could never purchase.
And when God gives you grace, never become proud of the gift and forget the Giver.

2. GRACE IS WHAT SUSTAINS THE JOURNEY.
Many people understand saving grace but forget sustaining grace.
We know God saved us, but sometimes we think we must now carry ourselves.
No!
The same grace that started you is the grace that keeps you.
Paul prayed three times concerning his weakness, and God answered in 2 Corinthians 12:9:
“My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”
God did not say, “Paul, become strong enough.”
He said, “My grace is sufficient.”
There are seasons when your strength will not be enough.
There are battles where your experience will not be enough.
There are doors that your connections cannot open.
There are moments when you will have to say:
“Father, if Your grace does not carry me, I cannot make it.”
And that is not weakness.
That is dependence on God.
EXAMPLE: ISRAEL IN THE WILDERNESS
Israel did not survive the wilderness because the wilderness was easy.
They survived because God sustained them.
He gave them manna.
He gave them water.
He gave them direction.
He gave them His presence.
The wilderness was difficult, but grace was present.
Never mistake a difficult season for the absence of God's grace.
Sometimes grace is not removing the wilderness.
Sometimes grace is giving you strength to cross it.

3. GRACE TEACHES US HOW TO LIVE.
Grace is not permission to remain the same.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace “teaches us to say ‘No’ to ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives.”
True grace does not make sin comfortable.
Grace changes our appetite.
Grace teaches you to walk differently.
Grace teaches you to forgive.
Grace teaches you to surrender.
Grace teaches you to say no when your flesh says yes.
Grace teaches you holiness.
Grace does not merely rescue you from the penalty of sin; it begins transforming the person who committed the sin.
That is why we must never use grace as an excuse for rebellion.
Grace is not God's permission to remain immature; grace is God's power to become transformed.

4. GRACE BRINGS US TO COMPLETION.
Philippians 1:6 gives us a powerful promise:
“He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.”
Look at the language:
He began.
He will carry it on.
He will complete it.
This means your life is not an unfinished accident.
God is working.
You may not see the finished picture, but the Artist has not put down His brush.
You may see pieces.
God sees the masterpiece.
You may see delay.
God sees development.
You may see weakness.
God sees what His grace is producing through the process.
ILLUSTRATION: A BUILDING UNDER CONSTRUCTION
When you pass a building under construction, you do not look at exposed bricks, cement, steel, and scaffolding and conclude that the architect has failed.
You understand that construction means the building is not finished yet.
Somebody needs to hear this:
You are still under construction.
Do not condemn yourself because God has not finished with you.
Do not allow people to define you by your unfinished state.
The same God who started the work has enough grace to finish it.

5. GRACE IS THE CROWN.
At the end of the journey, we will discover that everything was grace.
Paul says in 2 Timothy 4:7:
“I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.”
Paul finished.
Not because he never suffered.
Not because he never faced opposition.
Not because everything was easy.
He finished because grace sustained him.
And Revelation 2:10 says:
“Be faithful, even to the point of death, and I will give you life as your victor’s crown.”
The crown represents completion, victory, and reward.
But even the crown ultimately points back to God's grace.
Because if God had not kept you, you would not have finished.
If God had not strengthened you, you would have quit.
If God had not restored you, your failures would have buried you.
If God had not opened doors, you would not have entered them.
The crown may be placed on your head, but grace deserves the glory.

6. DON'T ABANDON GRACE FOR SELF-EFFORT.
Galatians 3:3 asks:
“After beginning by means of the Spirit, are you now trying to finish by means of the flesh?”
This is a dangerous temptation.
We start with prayer, then begin trusting our connections.
We start with dependence on God, then begin depending on ourselves.
We start by grace, then become proud of our achievements.
But the principle of the Kingdom remains:
What grace began, grace must sustain.
You cannot begin in God and finish in yourself.
You cannot receive the assignment by grace and complete it through pride.
You cannot enter through dependence and finish through self-sufficiency.

 DECLARATION
Lift your faith and declare:
I am a product of grace!
I am sustained by grace!
I am being transformed by grace!
I will not die in the middle of my assignment!
The grace that started me will sustain me!
The grace that sustained me will complete me!
And when I arrive at the place God ordained for me, I will return the glory to Him!

LESSONS FOR US TODAY
Never despise your beginning. God can start great things in ordinary places.
Never interpret difficulty as abandonment. Grace can sustain you in difficult seasons.
Never use grace as an excuse for sin. Grace teaches us to live differently.
Never compare your process with another person's process. God is completing His work in you.
Never take the glory for what only God could accomplish. Whatever we become, we become by His grace.
Never quit before the work is complete. The God who began the work is still working.

CONCLUSION
Beloved, grace is not merely the hand that pulled you out of the pit.
Grace is the hand that keeps you walking.
Grace is the strength when you are weak.
Grace is the wisdom when you do not know what to do.
Grace is the courage when you are afraid.
Grace is the restoration after failure.
Grace is the power to continue.
Grace is the assurance that God has not abandoned the work of His hands.
And one day, when the journey is finished, when the battles are over, when the assignment is complete, when we stand before our King, we will understand that from beginning to end, it was grace.
Grace began it.
Grace sustained it.
Grace completed it.
And grace will crown it.
So don't give up.
Don't go back.
Don't abandon the process.
Don't let your weakness convince you that God cannot finish what He started.
The grace that found you is still carrying you.
The grace that carried you this far will carry you to the finish line.
And when you finally wear the crown, make sure heaven hears your testimony:
“Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but to Your name be the glory.” — Psalm 115:1

After nearly 20 years in provider credentialing, payer enrollment, contracting, licensing and privileging, I launched The Credentialing Collective — bringing the experience I've gained behind the scenes for healthcare organizations directly to providers and practices that need experienced credentialing support.

I work with independent practices, medical groups, behavioral health organizations, urgent care, specialty practices, facilities and other healthcare organizations that need help getting providers and entities enrolled, contracted and operational — or simply need someone experienced enough to step in, figure out what's going wrong, and get things moving again.

My services include payer contracting and network participation, Medicare & Medicaid enrollment/revalidation, commercial payer enrollment, CAQH management, provider onboarding, licensing & privileging, facility/group enrollment, delegated rosters, EFT/ERA, demographic and ownership changes, payer research, appeals/escalations, credentialing clean-up projects, practice start-ups, and ongoing credentialing maintenance.

I've spent my career working through the complicated cases — navigating payer requirements, tracking down enrollment issues, solving problems, escalating when necessary, and keeping providers moving through systems that aren't always easy to navigate.

I also know there are a LOT of credentialers in these groups doing everything themselves. If you're overloaded, have a project outside your wheelhouse, need another experienced set of eyes, or have a client you can't take on, I'm happy to collaborate rather than compete.

And because anyone who has spent enough time in credentialing eventually develops a slightly questionable sense of humor 😂, The Credentialing Collective isn't going to be all business. I'm also building a place for credentialing education, resources, templates, tools, industry conversation and a little credentialing humor for the people who actually do this work.

If you have a credentialing problem that needs to be solved, a practice that needs to get contracted, providers who need to get enrolled, or a project your team simply doesn't have the bandwidth to handle — let's talk.

And if you know a provider, practice, healthcare organization, billing company or fellow credentialer who needs this kind of support, I'd appreciate the introduction.

Fellow credentialers — come follow along, too. I'd love for The Credentialing Collective to become a place where we can share what works, talk shop, laugh about what doesn't, and make this crazy payer world a little easier to navigate. 💙

items.postText:
Do not compare your journey with others, God writes a unique story for each soul,,,

Rev.Fr. Jerry Orbos, SVD

A GENTLE REMINDER FROM FR. JERRY ORBOS, SVD🙏 

“Do not compare your journey with others. God writes a unique story for each soul.”

Sometimes, we look at other people's lives and quietly wonder:

“Why am I not there yet?”

You see someone your age already achieving the things you are still praying for. Someone has a successful career, someone has already built a family, someone is traveling, someone is financially stable, while you are still trying to figure out what comes next.

And without realizing it, you begin to feel like you are falling behind.

But perhaps you are simply looking at someone else's chapter while forgetting to read your own.

God does not write everyone's story the same way.

Some people receive their blessings early. Others have to wait. Some find their direction quickly, while others spend years searching. Some doors open easily, while others have to knock many times before one finally opens.

That does not mean God loves one person more than another.

It simply means your journey is different.

You were never asked to live someone else's life.

You were never asked to reach their milestones at the same age, have the same achievements, or follow the same path.

🙏 Your life has its own timing.

Maybe right now, you are in a season of waiting. Maybe you are rebuilding yourself. Maybe you are starting over. Maybe you are praying for something that seems to be taking forever.

Don't let someone else's progress make you feel like a failure.

You don't know what God is preparing through the season you are currently in.

Sometimes, the waiting is preparing you.

Sometimes, the closed door is protecting you.

Sometimes, the delay is teaching you something you would never have learned if everything happened according to your plans.

And sometimes, what you think is a setback is actually God leading you somewhere you never expected to go.

So instead of constantly asking, “Why am I not where they are?”

Try asking:

“Lord, where are You leading me?”

That question changes everything.

Because when you stop comparing your journey with others, you begin to appreciate the blessings that are already in front of you.

You begin to notice how far you've come.

You begin to see the small victories, the answered prayers, the lessons, the people God has placed in your life, and even the struggles that made you stronger.

❤️ You are not behind. You are on your own journey.

Don't rush just because someone else is already ahead.

Don't lose gratitude because someone else has more.

Don't question your worth because another person's life looks better from where you stand.

Social media can show you someone's highlight, but it will never show you their entire story.

So keep walking.

Keep praying.

Keep doing your best.

And most importantly, keep trusting God.

The story He is writing for you does not have to look like anyone else's.

🙏 Your journey is uniquely yours. Your timing is uniquely yours. And God's plan for your life is not a competition.

One day, you may look back and realize that every delay, every detour, every unanswered prayer, and every season of waiting was part of a story God was carefully writing.

Don't compare your journey with others. Let God write your story. 🤍
